sweep_summary: Ewe (ewee1241) is in the catalog as tonal on Westermann 1907 §58. Six title hits, none a word-stress source. (1) Beavon-Ham 2020 'Prefix or prosody' — obtained the full open-access Festschrift PDF (12.9 MB) via an Internet Archive copy of the Leiden repository file (Leiden and Frankfurt servers bot-block automated download); 'prosody' = bisyllabic-minimality template for nouns and the low/toneless initial vowel; no stress statement — silent. (2) Fiedler & Jannedy 2013 (JALL 34) — paywalled; abstract read; the open 2006 CALL slides (Frankfurt repository) were downloaded and read: sentence-level F0/duration focus cues, Ewe focus mainly morphosyntactic; silent on word stress; Glottolog 676490 is a duplicate with year 1966. (3) Möhlig 1971 (Hamburger Beiträge zur Afrika-Kunde 14, pp. 132-141, German) — print-only (HathiTrust search-only uc1.b4411542, OCLC 377462); second-hand (Jannedy & Fiedler slide 5) it describes 'expressive prosodemes' realized by raising all high tones of an emphasized phrase; this is the one item worth acquiring (priority high) as the likely best first-hand prosodic statement for Standard Ewe. (4-5) Agawu 1995 and Neeley's 1997 review are ethnomusicology (Agawu's 'Rhythms of language' chapter unread; archive.org lending only). No item confirms, refines or contradicts the catalog's classification; no new first-hand stress statement found.

tone_statements.quote: Every syllable in Ewe bears a tone, i.e. the tone bearing unit (TBU) is the syllable. There are two underlying tones: the high toneme and the non-high toneme [5]. In root nouns, the high toneme can occur as a high tone or a mid tone (in Aŋlɔgbe, but as a mid-rising tone in Eʋedomegbe) depending on the onset of the syllable (1). ... Verbs in Tɔŋúgbé have a CV shape. They can be either high or low. ... There are four level tones in root nouns of Tɔŋúgbé. In addition to the three surface tones identified for Ewe, Tɔŋúgbé adds to the list a fourth level tone. We mark this fourth level tone as [ˊˊ] and label it as ‘superhigh’

tone_statements.citation: Peng, Long. 1995. Voice asymmetry in Ewe nouns. Studies in African Linguistics 24(1): 70-80.
tone_statements.quote: Ewe has three surface tones: H, M, L. Combining three tones with voiced, voiceless, and sonorant onsets predicts nine patterns of monomoraic nouns. Five are attested in (2). Significantly, voiceless and sonorant onsets do not cooccur with a following low tone, while voiced obstruents do not appear with either a high or mid tone. ... Tonal distributions of Ewe monosyllabic nouns are completely predictable. I propose that monomoraic and bimoraic nouns are not specified for any tone in underlying representation. High and low tones are derived by phonological rules; mid tones surface as default.

tone_statements.quote: In the Ewe language, for example, the word to [H] pronounced with a high tone means 'ear' ... But as soon as the high tone is replaced by a low one the meaning of the word changes drastically: to [L] means 'thick' ... In line 2 I have for convenience's sake kept the speech tones within a three-tone framework, low, mid and high. There are, in addition, two contour tones, falling and rising. Although opinions differ as to the number of tones in Ewe (Ansre, 1961, argues for a two-tone framework while Fiagbedzi, 1979: 18, suggests a three-tone framework for Anlo-Ewe), it ultimately does not matter how many levels of tone we choose.

tone_statements.quote: Traditional analyses of Ewe tone (Westermann, Berry, Welmers) have set up three levels of tonemes: High, Mid, and Low, and two compound, or kinetic, tonemes: Rising and Falling. ... it seems to me that with a number of relatively minor exceptions all of the phonetic tones of Ewe can be predicted by rule from knowledge of the underlying form of each lexical item, provided this includes the location of "high tone" (+H) or accent. This is clearly true for the level tones, less obviously so for the kinetic tones. I would claim, however, that in the underlying form of Ewe words there is no rising or falling tone. Phonetically, kinetic tones arise from sequences of vowels ...

tone_statements.summary: Generative reanalysis: only [+High] ('high tone or accent', p. 290) is lexically marked, usually on the last vowel; mid/low follow by ordered rules; rising/falling = two-vowel sequences. No own count.

sources.quote: In this article I consider the initial vowels on monomorphemic nouns in the Gbe languages, looking specifically at how they have developed such that synchronically they play a phonological role rather than a semantic or syntactic role (such as that of a noun class prefix). In many of the Gbe varieties, the initial vowel must be present to satisfy the templatic constraint that nouns be minimally bisyllabic. [...] This article concludes with a discussion of how prosodic considerations in Gbe have become primordial in determining the form of nouns.

sources.note: Nothing. The words stress/accent do not occur in the chapter except in a reference-list title (Clements 1978 in Napoli ed., Elements of Tone, Stress, and Intonation). Silent on word-stress placement in Ewe.

sources.quote: It has often been claimed that in tone languages such as Ewe, prosodic devices are not exploited in order to mark information-structural categories. The present study therefore investigates, on the basis of an experimental study, whether there is an impact of different focus structures (all-new utterances, in situ object focus, ex situ object focus and subject focus) on the prosodic realization of utterances in this language. The basic prosodic cues we have looked at are F0 variation and duration. From this study we can conclude that focus in Ewe is in fact also expressed prosodically. [...] These effects can however be argued to play a secondary role to morphological marking and ex situ positioning.

Nothing on where word stress falls. The 2013 paper's background section (unread) might restate the absence of lexical stress but is not a primary stress source.

tone.quote: Traditional analyses of Ewe tone (Westermann, Berry, Welmers) have set up three levels of tonemes: High, Mid, and Low, and two compound, or kinetic, tonemes: Rising and Falling. ... it seems to me that with a number of relatively minor exceptions all of the phonetic tones of Ewe can be predicted by rule from knowledge of the underlying form of each lexical item, provided this includes the location of "high tone" (+H) or accent. This is clearly true for the level tones, less obviously so for the kinetic tones. I would claim, however, that in the underlying form of Ewe words there is no rising or falling tone. Phonetically, kinetic tones arise from sequences of vowels ...
tone.locator: QPR No. 88 p. 290, section XXXI.B 'Tone in Ewe', opening paragraphs; superscript footnote numerals 1-7 omitted
tone.summary: Generative reanalysis: only [+High] ('high tone or accent', p. 290) is lexically marked, usually on the last vowel; mid/low follow by ordered rules; rising/falling = two-vowel sequences. No own count.
